claim: Bichirs represent the earliest diverged living group of ray-finned fishes.
source: Polypterid bichirs represent the earliest diverged living group of ray-finned (Actinopterygian) fishes (Hughes et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2018

claim: Bichirs possess ventral paired lungs.
source: Adult bichirs possess several intriguing characteristics that have been associated with air-breathing during the transition from water to land, such as ventral paired lungs or spiracular openings on the head (Clack, 2007; Coates and Clack, 1991; Graham et al., 2014; Tatsumi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Bichirs possess larval external gills.
source: Moreover, bichirs also share several key larval features with lungfishes or amphibians, such as cranial adhesive organs, and larval external gills (Kerr, 1907; Diedhiou and Bartsch, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kerr, 1907 and Diedhiou and Bartsch, 2009

claim: External gills of bichirs represent major breathing organs of their free-living embryos and early larvae.
source: The external gills of bichirs represent prominent adaptive structures, and constitute major breathing organs of their free-living embryos and early larvae (Figure 1A) (Kerr, 1907; Diedhiou and Bartsch, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A showing external gills

claim: External gills of amphibians and lungfishes derive from branchial arches.
source: Strikingly, while external gills of amphibians and lungfishes derive from branchial arches as a rule (Duellman and Trueb, 1994; Witzmann, 2004; Nokhbatolfoghahai and Downie, 2008; Schoch and Witzmann, 2011)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: External gills of bichirs have historically been considered as hyoid arch derivatives due to their blood supply from the hyoid aortic arch.
source: those of bichirs have historically been considered as unique hyoid arch derivatives due to their blood supply from the hyoid aortic arch (Kerr, 1907; Goodrich, 1909).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical literature

claim: External gills of bichir embryos represent the first cranial structures to appear, emerging before the eyes or mouth are evident.
source: Importantly, the external gills of bichir embryos represent the first cranial structures to appear, emerging before the eyes or mouth are evident (Figure 1B) (Minarik et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 1B showing early external gills

claim: The first sign of external gill development is a pair of outgrowths situated lateral to the closing neural folds.
source: The first sign of external gill development is a pair of outgrowths situated lateral to the closing neural folds (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1C showing the outgrowths

claim: The hyoid origin of external gill outgrowths is suggested by the expression pattern of Hoxa2.
source: The hyoid origin of these outgrowths is suggested by the expression pattern of the Hoxa2 (Figure 1D), a selector gene characteristic of hyoid identity in other vertebrates (Rijli et al., 1993; Hunter and Prince, 2002; Baltzinger et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by Hoxa2 expression data in Figure 1D and citations establishing Hoxa2 as a hyoid marker

claim: Hoxa2 is a selector gene characteristic of hyoid identity in vertebrates.
source: a selector gene characteristic of hyoid identity in other vertebrates (Rijli et al., 1993; Hunter and Prince, 2002; Baltzinger et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: In bichir embryos, the hyoid neural crest segment forms concurrently with the mandibular neural crest segment.
source: In bichir embryos, Sox9 expression pattern reveals that the hyoid neural crest segment is developmentally advanced, as it forms concurrently with the mandibular neural crest segment (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by Sox9 expression data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Mandibular neural crest cells still reside within the neuroepithelium while hyoid neural crest cells have already emigrated from the neural folds.
source: Sections through the neural folds, however, demonstrate that mandibular neural crest cells still reside within the neuroepithelium (Figure 2B), while the hyoid neural crest cells have already emigrated from the neural folds (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by histological sections shown in Figures 2B and 2C

claim: The hyoid neural crest stream is much larger when compared to the mandibular neural crest stream.
source: Later in migration, the hyoid neural crest stream remains predominant (Figure 2D), as it is much larger when compared to the mandibular neural crest stream (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by comparative data shown in Figures 2D, 2E, and 2F

claim: The majority of the mesenchyme in the early bichir head appears to arise from the hyoid neural crest stream.
source: The hyoid neural crest stream still progresses at later stages (Figure 2G), and as such, the majority of the mesenchyme in the early bichir head appears to arise from this source (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 2G and 2H

claim: Cells of the leading edge of the hyoid stream delaminate from the neural folds prior to the emigration of the mandibular stream.
source: The Sox9 immunoreactivity further shows that cells of the leading edge of the hyoid stream delaminate from the neural folds prior to the emigration of the mandibular stream (Figure 2I)
evidence: Supported by Sox9 immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 2I

claim: Hyoid neural crest cells populate the fully developed and functional external gills.
source: After hatching, the CM-DiI-positive cells populate the fully developed and functional external gills (Figure 2N,O).
evidence: Supported by fate mapping data shown in Figures 2N and 2O

claim: Bichir external gills are populated by the cells of the hyoid neural crest stream.
source: Thus, our fate mapping experiment confirms that bichir external gills are, indeed, populated by the cells of the hyoid neural crest stream and, implicitly, that they represent hyoid arch derivatives.
evidence: Supported by fate mapping experiments described in the manuscript

claim: Cranial neural crest cells have a major influence on the differentiation and morphogenesis of the cranial myogenic mesoderm.
source: In vertebrates, cranial neural crest cells are the primary source of craniofacial mesenchyme, but also have a major influence on the differentiation and morphogenesis of the cranial myogenic mesoderm (Ericsson et al., 2004; Tokita and Schneider, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The first muscles in the cranial region of bichir embryos form within the hyoid arch and are associated with the external gills.
source: However, within the cranial region of bichir embryos, the earliest developing muscles form within the hyoid arch and are associated with the external gills (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by muscle staining data shown in Figures 3B and 3C

claim: The first muscle complex in bichir embryos is situated lateral to the otic vesicle and connects filaments of the external gills to the gill stem.
source: This first muscle complex (levator and depressor branchiarum, Noda et al., 2017) is situated lateral to the otic vesicle and connects filaments of the external gills to the gill stem (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figures 3B-D and citation to Noda et al., 2017

claim: The external gill-associated muscles are innervated from the hyo-opercular ramus of the facial nerve.
source: The premature differentiation of the external gill-associated muscles is further supported by their innervation from the hyo-opercular ramus of the facial nerve, allowing voluntary movement of external gills from the earliest larval stages (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by nerve staining data shown in Figures 3E and 3F

claim: Bichir embryos display unique heterochrony in the differentiation of the hyoid over the mandibular arch mesoderm.
source: Thus, bichir embryos display unique heterochrony in the differentiation of the hyoid over the mandibular arch mesoderm, providing muscular supports for their external gills.
evidence: Inferred from the developmental timing data presented in the manuscript

claim: The pharyngeal endoderm forms two pairs of early outpocketings in bichir embryos.
source: Reconstruction of the endodermal epithelium of the bichir pharynx using micro-CT imaging (Minarik et al., 2017) reveals that the pharyngeal endoderm forms two pairs of early outpocketings (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT imaging data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The posterior paired outpocketings constitute primordia of the external gills.
source: Whereas the rostral pair represents the embryonic precursor of the cement glands (Figure 4A–D,F–I) (Minarik et al., 2017), the posterior paired outpocketings constitute primordia of the external gills (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT imaging data shown in Figures 4A-D

claim: The hyoid endodermal outpocketings constitute a substantial proportion of the external gill primordium.
source: Transverse sections confirm that these hyoid endodermal outpocketings constitute a substantial proportion of the external gill primordium (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by histological sections shown in Figure 4E

claim: The endodermal outpocketing constitutes a considerable portion of the developing external gill.
source: Thus, while ectoderm covers the entire external gill primordium, the endodermal outpocketing constitutes a considerable portion of the developing external gill (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Morphogenesis of the pharyngeal pouches is critically regulated by factors from many signaling pathways.
source: Morphogenesis of the pharyngeal pouches is critically regulated by factors from many signaling pathways (Graham and Smith, 2001; Graham, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Alterations in Fibroblast growth factor (Fgf) signaling lead to defects in proper endodermal pouch development and pharyngeal segmentation.
source: among which alterations in Fibroblast growth factor (Fgf) signaling lead to defects in proper endodermal pouch development and pharyngeal segmentation (Jandzik et al., 2014; Abu-Issa et al., 2002; Crump et al., 2004; Walshe and Mason, 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Fgf8 expression is present in endodermal outpocketings and becomes confined to their lateral portions.
source: Fgf8 expression is present in endodermal outpocketings and becomes confined to their lateral portions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Fgf8 expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Expression of Dusp6 and Pea3 are present in the external gill mesenchyme adjacent to the outgrowing endodermal tips.
source: Expression of Dusp6 and Pea3 (the Fgf signaling pathway readouts) and antibody localization for activated MAPK (marker of active Fgf signaling) are present in the external gill mesenchyme adjacent to the outgrowing endodermal tips or both in the mesenchyme and the endodermal tips (Figure 4L–N; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and antibody staining data shown in Figures 4L-N and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The endodermal epithelium signals to the adjacent mesenchyme through Fgf signaling to regulate outgrowth of the external gill.
source: The topographical relation of endodermal outpocketings and the direction of Fgf signaling within the external gill primordium thus suggest that the endodermal epithelium signals to the adjacent mesenchyme through Fgf signaling to regulate outgrowth of the external gill (Figure 4O).
evidence: Inferred from the spatial expression patterns of Fgf signaling components

claim: Disrupting Fgf signaling perturbs morphogenesis of the hyoid endodermal outpocketings and leads to the loss of the external gill primordia.
source: In contrast to control embryos displaying well-developed hyoid endodermal outpocketings and external gill primordia (18/18, Figure 4P–Q), disrupting Fgf signaling perturbs morphogenesis of the hyoid endodermal outpocketings and leads to the loss of the external gill primordia (14/15, Figure 4R–S) possibly due to the loss of expression of downstream genes (Figure 4T–U).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figures 4P-U

claim: The pharyngeal endoderm plays a central role in triggering early development of bichir external gills.
source: These results support a central role of the pharyngeal endoderm in triggering early development of bichir external gills.
evidence: Inferred from the Fgf signaling inhibition experiments

claim: External gills are commonly considered as outer surface structures composed of ectoderm.
source: The pharyngeal origin of the external gill primordia is surprising given that the external gills are commonly considered as outer surface structures composed of ectoderm (Takeuchi et al., 2009; Diedhiou and Bartsch, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: True, internal gills of vertebrates typically form as pharyngeal endodermal structures.
source: However, our finding of an endodermal component in the early formation of bichir external gills reveals an unanticipated similarity with the true, internal gills of vertebrates, which typically form as pharyngeal endodermal structures (Warga and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1999; Gillis and Tidswell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The sequential formation of pharyngeal segments during embryonic development has deep deuterostome origins.
source: The sequential formation of pharyngeal segments during embryonic development has deep deuterostome origins (Willey, 1891; Koop et al., 2014; Gillis et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Sequential formation of pharyngeal segments is well conserved among vertebrates.
source: and it is well conserved among vertebrates, where all the embryonic cranial segments typically follow the sequential anteroposterior order during development (Quinlan et al., 2004; Grevellec and Tucker, 2010; Schilling, 2008; Santagati and Rijli, 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Bichir embryos diverge from the common vertebrate developmental scheme by the profoundly accelerated development of the second, hyoid segment.
source: Bichir embryos diverge from this common scheme by the profoundly accelerated development of the second, hyoid segment, with earlier and orchestrated formation of the endodermal, mesodermal, and neural crest tissues (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by the developmental data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 5

claim: The heterochronic shift in the anteroposterior sequence constitutes a developmental basis for the early appearance of external gills.
source: This unique heterochronic shift in the anteroposterior sequence constitutes a developmental basis for the early appearance of external gills that represent key breathing organs of bichir free-living embryos and early larvae.
evidence: Inferred from the developmental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Bichir external gills significantly differ from the external gills of amphibian and lungfish larvae that characteristically supplement the post-hyoid, branchial arches.
source: Bichir external gills significantly differ from the external gills of amphibian and lungfish larvae that characteristically supplement the post-hyoid, branchial arches (Duellman and Trueb, 1994; Witzmann, 2004; Nokhbatolfoghahai and Downie, 2008; Schoch and Witzmann, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and comparison with bichir data

claim: The hyoid segmental origin of bichir external gills suggests an independent evolution of bichir external gills.
source: The hyoid segmental origin represents a major developmental dissimilarity and suggests an independent evolution of bichir external gills.
evidence: Inferred from the developmental differences between bichir and other vertebrate external gills

claim: Bichir external gills likely correspond to opercular structures that in ray-finned fishes typically form as caudal expansions of the hyoid arch.
source: Developmentally, bichir external gills likely correspond to opercular structures that in ray-finned fishes typically form as caudal expansions of the hyoid arch to cover the gill-bearing branchial arches, and that persist in amniotes as early embryonic opercular flaps (Richardson et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from developmental homology and supported by citation

claim: In bichirs, the opercular flap forms directly from the base of their external gills.
source: In bichirs, the opercular flap forms directly from the base of their external gills, and it progressively expands during early larval stages while external gills become reduced (Diedhiou and Bartsch, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diedhiou and Bartsch, 2009

claim: In adult bichirs, the hyoid domain contributes to air-breathing by forming paired spiracular chamber with openings located on the dorsal surface of the skull.
source: Moreover, in adult bichirs, the hyoid domain also contributes to air-breathing by forming paired spiracular chamber with openings located on the dorsal surface of the skull (Graham et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graham et al., 2014

claim: Bichirs are unique across recent vertebrates in enhancing breathing capacity through the development of several structures associated with the hyoid cranial segment.
source: Bichirs thus seem unique across recent vertebrates in enhancing breathing capacity through the development of several structures associated with the hyoid cranial segment.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple hyoid-derived breathing structures described in the manuscript

claim: In most vertebrates, pharyngeal arches form in a stereotypic anterior-to-posterior progression.
source: In most vertebrates, pharyngeal arches form in a stereotypic anterior-to-posterior progression.
evidence: Represents established knowledge in developmental biology

claim: The first, or mandibular arch contributes to the jaws in the majority of jawed vertebrates.
source: In the majority of jawed vertebrates, the first, or mandibular arch contributes to the jaws
evidence: Represents established knowledge in developmental biology

claim: The second, or hyoid arch serves as the jaw support in the majority of jawed vertebrates.
source: the second, or hyoid arch serves as the jaw support
evidence: Represents established knowledge in developmental biology

claim: The more posterior branchial arches typically bear internal pharyngeal gills in the majority of jawed vertebrates.
source: and the more posterior branchial arches typically bear internal pharyngeal gills.
evidence: Represents established knowledge in developmental biology

claim: Pharyngeal arches form in a highly stereotyped sequence from anterior to posterior in most vertebrates.
source: Pharyngeal arches form in a highly stereotyped sequence from anterior to posterior, where the contacts between endodermal pouches and surface ectoderm physically separate the mesoderm- and neural crest-derived arch tissues (Graham and Smith, 2001; Shone and Graham, 2014; Choe and Crump, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The progressive development of the pharynx has deep deuterostome origins.
source: The progressive development of the pharynx has deep deuterostome origins, as it is characteristic of both cephalochordates and hemichordates (Willey, 1891; Gillis et al., 2012; Koop et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Sequential formation of pharyngeal segments represents a fundamental aspect of the metameric organization of the head and face in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, sequential formation of pharyngeal segments represents a fundamental aspect of the metameric organization of the head and face (Piotrowski and Nüsslein-Volhard, 2000; Couly et al., 2002; Choe and Crump, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Modifications of the anteroposterior differentiation scheme would represent a radical alteration in development of the stereotypic chordate bauplan.
source: Any modifications of this well-established anteroposterior differentiation scheme would represent a radical alteration in development of the stereotypic chordate bauplan (Square et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Square et al., 2017

claim: Bichirs are often referred to as the most relevant species for studying character states at the dichotomy of ray- and lobe-finned fishes.
source: and they are often referred to as the most relevant species for studying character states at the dichotomy of ray- and lobe-finned fishes (e.g., Standen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Standen et al., 2014

claim: Bichirs are in a unique phylogenetic position among vertebrates that can be exploited for evolutionary and developmental comparative studies.
source: This places bichirs in a unique phylogenetic position among vertebrates, which can be exploited for evolutionary and developmental comparative studies (e.g., Takeuchi et al., 2009; Standen et al., 2014; Minarik et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Adult bichirs possess spiracular openings on the head.
source: Adult bichirs possess several intriguing characteristics that have been associated with air-breathing during the transition from water to land, such as ventral paired lungs or spiracular openings on the head (Clack, 2007; Coates and Clack, 1991; Graham et al., 2014; Tatsumi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Bichirs share cranial adhesive organs with lungfishes or amphibians.
source: Moreover, bichirs also share several key larval features with lungfishes or amphibians, such as cranial adhesive organs, and larval external gills (Kerr, 1907; Diedhiou and Bartsch, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Sox9 is a transcription factor critical for neural crest cell emergence, migration, and differentiation.
source: As a marker for migrating neural crest cells, we used expression of Sox9, a transcription factor critical for their emergence, migration, and differentiation (Cheung and Briscoe, 2003; Mori-Akiyama et al., 2003; Theveneau and Mayor, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Rhombomere 4 is the source of the prospective hyoid neural crest stream in other vertebrates.
source: We directly tested whether the hyoid neural crest cell stream contributes to the external gills by performing focal CM-DiI injections into rhombomere 4 (Figure 2L inset), the source of the prospective hyoid neural crest stream in other vertebrates (Lumsden et al., 1991; Köntges and Lumsden, 1996; Minoux and Rijli, 2010; Theveneau and Mayor, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: One day after neurulation, CM-DiI-positive hyoid neural crest cells are observed all along the proximodistal axis of the external gill primordium.
source: One day after neurulation, the CM-DiI-positive hyoid neural crest cells are observed all along the proximodistal axis of the external gill primordium (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by fate mapping data shown in Figure 2L

claim: Two days after neurulation, CM-DiI-positive cells occupy the primary branches of the external gills in 16 out of 21 specimens.
source: Two days later, they occupy the primary branches of the external gills (16/21, Figure 2M).
evidence: Supported by fate mapping data shown in Figure 2M

claim: The first muscles differentiate stereotypically from the post-otic somites in the trunk region in bichir embryos.
source: Whole-mount antibody staining against skeletal muscle marker 12/101 revealed that the first muscles differentiate stereotypically from the post-otic somites in the trunk region, as in other vertebrates (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by muscle staining data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Other cranial muscles fully differentiate only at later larval stages when the external gill muscle complex becomes supplemented by other muscles of hyoid and mandibular origins.
source: Other cranial muscles fully differentiate only at later larval stages when the external gill muscle complex becomes supplemented by other muscles of hyoid and mandibular origins (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by muscle staining data shown in Figure 3G

claim: The first pharyngeal pouch (mandibulo-hyoid, or spiracular) is situated rostrally to the external gill primordia.
source: These posterior outpocketings belong to the hyoid segment, as the first pharyngeal pouch (mandibulo-hyoid, or spiracular) is situated rostrally (Figure 4C,D, white arrowhead)
evidence: Supported by micro-CT imaging data shown in Figures 4C and 4D

claim: The second pharyngeal pouch (hyoid-branchial) is situated caudally to the external gill primordia.
source: and the second pharyngeal pouch (hyoid-branchial) more caudally (Figure 4H, black arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT imaging data shown in Figure 4H

claim: At later stages, hyoid endodermal outpocketings transform into pocket-like structures that become supplemented with mesenchymal cells of the hyoid neural crest stream.
source: At later stages, these outpocketings further transform into pocket-like structures (Figure 4G,H,J) that become supplemented with mesenchymal cells of the hyoid neural crest stream (Figure 2L–N).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT imaging and fate mapping data

claim: Pharyngeal morphogenesis might represent a central developmental component of vertebrate gill breathing organs irrespective of their actual topographic position.
source: Pharyngeal morphogenesis might thus represent a central developmental component of vertebrate gill breathing organs irrespective of their actual topographic position.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the similarity between bichir external gills and internal gills

claim: The hyoid-opercular ramus of the facial nerve allows voluntary movement of external gills from the earliest larval stages.
source: The premature differentiation of the external gill-associated muscles is further supported by their innervation from the hyo-opercular ramus of the facial nerve, allowing voluntary movement of external gills from the earliest larval stages (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Inferred from the innervation pattern shown in Figures 3E and 3F

claim: The hyoid arch-derived external gills and opercular flaps are both engaged in breathing and gill ventilation in bichir larvae.
source: Interestingly, the hyoid arch-derived external gills and opercular flaps are both engaged in breathing and gill ventilation in bichir larvae.
evidence: Inferred from the developmental and functional relationships described

claim: In bichir embryos, the entire hyoid arch segment is accelerated with earlier and orchestrated development of the endodermal, mesodermal, and neural crest tissues.
source: In bichir embryos, we find that the anteroposterior way of formation of cranial segments is modified by the unique acceleration of the entire hyoid arch segment, with earlier and orchestrated development of the endodermal, mesodermal, and neural crest tissues.
evidence: Supported by the developmental data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: This major heterochronic shift in the anteroposterior developmental sequence enables early appearance of the external gills.
source: This major heterochronic shift in the anteroposterior developmental sequence enables early appearance of the external gills that represent key breathing organs of bichir free-living embryos and early larvae.
evidence: Inferred from the developmental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Bichirs stay as unique models for understanding developmental mechanisms facilitating increased breathing capacity.
source: Bichirs thus stay as unique models for understanding developmental mechanisms facilitating increased breathing capacity.
evidence: Inferred from the unique developmental features described in the manuscript
